_comment: Kitchen answers to questions the Weekly Stock Check workbook cannot answer.
Every entry is something a person decided, not something a script derived,
so each one records who said it and when. The importer applies these on top
of the workbook and reports any that no longer match a catalog row.
base_unit      the unit the item is measured in, where the workbook tracks
neither a loose unit nor a unit count.
case           how a supplier's case breaks down. Either per_case plus
item_size and item_unit for a case of discrete things, or
case_size and case_unit for bulk sold by weight with no
countable item inside it.
needs_health_mark  whether the item's label carries the oval health mark.
It follows animal origin, so it sits on the raw meat and
bone ingredients rather than on the products made from
them. Anything absent from this file stays null, meaning
not yet determined rather than no mark.
An entry may also create an item the workbook does not have at all. Those
carry an explicit id, kind and base_unit, and their ids are prefixed
`trace:` so it is obvious at a glance which rows came from the workbook
and which this project minted.
locations and suppliers are listed here in full rather than derived: the
workbook records a storage word per ingredient and two sites, but never
which physical areas exist. Only Glasgow is in scope.
after_opening states how an item must be kept once opened. Dean's rule is
that it matches the unopened requirement everywhere except the items
listed as exceptions, which move to the fridge. The rule is applied only
where the unopened requirement is known, so products, which have none,
stay null on both.
product_storage covers the finished products, which the workbook records
no storage for at all. The frozen lines and the shelf-stable oils and
sauces are named; everything else goes to the walk-in fridge.

case.reason: sold per kg, so there is no fixed case size to convert from
